title: Instagram Offers Creators Up to $500,000 for Videos Without YouTube-Style Revenue Share
excerpt: Meta is funding invited creators to seed Features, its 90-minute video format, but has no advertising revenue share to offer the wider creator community yet.
body:
• Instagram is testing Features, a format for horizontal videos up to 90 minutes long, aimed at podcasts, interviews and comedy specials.
  • Selected creators have reportedly been offered between $50,000 and $500,000 in private, non-exclusive deals to post long-form videos, according to Business Insider reporting.
  • There is no YouTube-style advertising revenue share yet: YouTube pays partners 55% of net ad revenue on long-form videos, while Instagram says its long-term monetisation model is not settled.
  • For creators, the deals are invite-only launch incentives, not an open income stream — anyone not in the test currently earns nothing from Features views alone.

Instagram wants creators to post their longest videos on Instagram. The Meta-owned platform is testing a format called Features, which supports horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes, and it is reportedly paying selected creators between $50,000 and $500,000 to supply them, according to Business Insider reporting summarised by DesignTAXI. The question the offers leave open is whether long-form work can pay on Instagram once the cheques stop.

How Features Works

Features is built for the formats that do not fit a Reel: podcasts, interviews, documentaries, comedy specials and episodic programmes. Creators can link up to eight short Reels clips to one full-length video, so a viewer who meets a highlight in the feed can continue to the complete programme without leaving Instagram, TheStreet reported. "You see a clip of a podcast that you love, you can just click and continue watching," Instagram product vice president Tessa Lyons said. The test began with some long-form creators in Brazil and a small group in the United States, and Instagram plans to expand access to tens of thousands of US creators over the coming months. The videos are also headed to Instagram's TV app.

The Money, and What Is Missing

Meta has confirmed it is directly funding Features content from a limited group of creators, but it has not disclosed how many videos each agreement covers, how long the contracts run, or how payments are calculated. The reported arrangements do not demand exclusivity: participants can keep uploading to YouTube, with at least some asked to release comparable long-form content on Instagram on the same day. What Features does not have is a general advertising revenue-sharing programme. A Meta spokesperson said it was "too early to share a long-term monetisation model," and Instagram head Adam Mosseri has acknowledged that the economics matter and that the company is exploring options to help long-form creators earn.

"We spend more money than we make back by a long shot."

— Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram, on the platform's existing creator payments

The YouTube Comparison

The comparison creators are making is with YouTube's Partner Program, which pays eligible creators 55% of net advertising revenue on long-form videos and 45% of a shared pool for Shorts. YouTube has said it paid out more than $100 billion to creators, artists and media companies over four years. Against that, some creators are openly sceptical of Features. "If people can watch my long-form on Instagram instead of YouTube, am I cannibalising my AdSense?" creator Vanessa Lau asked, as TheStreet reported. Others see reach itself as the payment: "Attention and discovery are forms of currency," said Samir of The Colin and Samir Show. Instagram's position is that brand partnerships can fill part of the gap — Lyons has said creators may carry existing sponsorships into Features videos, and that Instagram intends to help creators without such relationships find deals.

What to Watch

Instagram has been here before: it discontinued IGTV, its earlier long-form product, in 2022. Features differs in using Reels — the format that already commands attention on the platform — as the funnel into longer viewing. Whether it becomes a durable home for long video will depend less on the reported six-figure launch deals, which reach only a small invited group, than on whether Meta builds the open, predictable revenue share that lets ordinary creators, including the many Indian and diaspora podcasters and comedians now publishing on YouTube, treat an Instagram view as income rather than exposure.
nri_angle: Indian and diaspora podcasters and comedians earn predictable income from YouTube's revenue share; Features offers them reach and invite-only deals, but no open per-view income yet.
author: Diaspora Desk
